item.research_question: How do the microstructure, phase formation, and corrosion properties of AlCrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy coatings differ when prepared by high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) versus high-velocity air fuel (HVAF) thermal spraying?
item.material_system: Equimolar AlCrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (feedstock produced by inert gas atomization)
item.processing_route: Thermal spraying using HVOF (K2 liquid-fueled system) and HVAF (M3TM-HVAF system with 4L4C nozzle, 250 mm length, 22.75 mm exit diameter) on mild steel substrates (EN 1.0045) grit blasted at 2.5 bar, 70° angle; HVOF used -45 +15 µm powder, HVAF used -33 +15 µm powder
item.test_conditions: Potentiodynamic polarization in 0.5 M NaCl and 0.05 M H2SO4 aerated electrolytes at room temperature; surface interrupted at 2 mA/cm2 for microscopy; microhardness HV 0.1; roughness Ra, Rz; porosity via optical microscopy
key_findings: Porosity reduced from 0.6 ± 0.2% in HVOF coatings to 0.3 ± 0.1% in HVAF coatings
Microhardness increased from 600 ± 50 HV 0.1 (HVOF) to 680 ± 20 HV 0.1 (HVAF)
Surface roughness decreased from Ra: 4.6 ± 0.1 µm (HVOF) to Ra: 4.0 ± 0.2 µm (HVAF)
Corrosion current density (icorr) reduced by a factor of two in HVAF coatings compared to HVOF in NaCl electrolyte
Passivation current density in H2SO4 reduced to 0.013 mA/cm2 for HVAF vs. 0.073 mA/cm2 for HVOF
Pitting potential remained similar for both coatings (947 mV for HVOF vs. 957 mV for HVAF)
No distinct oxide lamellae formed in HVAF coatings due to reduced thermal input
Metastable bcc (B2) structure retained in both coating types with lattice parameter a = 2.87 Å
item.mechanism: The reduced thermal input in HVAF spraying suppresses oxygen pick-up and oxide formation, leading to lower porosity and a denser microstructure. The finer powder fraction used in HVAF results in decreased grain size and increased hardness. The improved corrosion resistance and passivation behavior in HVAF coatings are attributed to the formation of a denser and more protective passive layer, likely due to the reduced structural defects and lower oxide content.
item.limitations: No passivation was observed in either coating type when tested in 0.5 M NaCl electrolyte; extensive delamination and coating failure occurred at high current densities in NaCl; the study was limited to as-sprayed conditions without post-deposition heat treatment.
item.future_work: The authors state that the HVAF process shows high potential for processing HEAs and imply further investigation into optimizing parameters for even better defect reduction and corrosion resistance, though specific future experiments are not detailed beyond the general potential of the process.
quotes: Precipitation reactions are suppressed by the rapid solidification during atomization and by the relatively low thermal input during spraying.

In the passive region, the HVAF coatings show a lower mean current density (0.013 vs. 0.073 mA/cm2) compared to the HVOF coatings, which indicates the formation of a denser and more protective passive layer.
The coating process of HVAF thermal spraying shows a high potential for the processing of HEAs, enabling the production of coatings with reduced structural defects and increased hardness.
